name: Unlawful killing of another person
plain: A person is killed by another person, and the law doesn't excuse it.

name: The act caused the death
plain: The person's act was a real cause of the death: without it the person wouldn't have died, and a reasonably careful person could have seen that it would probably lead to that result. It doesn't have to be the only cause.
note: Listed as a separate thing the State must prove in N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206.10, 206.15, 206.41 and 206.50.

name: Malice
plain: Not just hatred or ill will. It also means the state of mind that leads a person to intentionally take a life, or to intentionally cause serious bodily harm that results in death, without justification. An act so reckless that it shows no regard for human life can also count.
note: G.S. 14-17(b) uses the word but the meaning comes from court decisions. Wording follows N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206.10. That instruction also lets a jury infer malice from an intentional killing with a deadly weapon; that is evidence guidance, so it isn't shown here.

name: Premeditated and deliberate
plain: Premeditation: the person formed the intent to kill over some period of time, however short, before acting. Deliberation: the person acted in a cool state of mind, not under a suddenly aroused violent passion. A total absence of emotion isn't required.
note: The statute says 'willful, deliberate, and premeditated'. These definitions follow N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206.10, which lists premeditation and deliberation as separate things the State must prove.

name: Killing by a specified method
plain: The killing was done by one of the methods the statute names: poison, lying in wait, imprisonment, starving, torture, or a nuclear, biological, or chemical weapon of mass destruction.

name: Killing during a listed felony
plain: The death happened while the person was committing, or trying to commit, arson, rape or a sex offense, robbery, kidnapping, burglary, or another felony using a deadly weapon.

name: Not first-degree murder
plain: The killing doesn't meet any of the first-degree routes.

name: Inherently dangerous act (malice basis)
plain: The malice rests on an act or failure to act that is inherently dangerous and done so recklessly and wantonly that it shows a mind utterly without regard for human life and social duty, and deliberately bent on mischief. This is what makes second-degree murder a lower class (B2 instead of B1).

name: Intent to kill
plain: The person meant to cause the death.
note: In the assault offenses this is a specific intent to kill (N.C.P.I.-Crim. 208.10). The homicide offenses don't require it.

name: A deliberate act likely to cause death or serious injury
plain: The act that caused the death was done on purpose, and it was an assault that is itself a felony or is likely to cause death or serious injury. It doesn't mean the person meant to kill.
note: N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206.10, footnote 21 (citing State v. Ray): 'intentional killing' refers to the act, not to a specific intent to kill.

name: No intent to kill
plain: The person didn't mean to cause the death.

name: Death was unintended
plain: The person didn't mean to cause the death.
note: The act that caused the death can itself be intentional or not (N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206.10, n.21). What matters is that the act isn't a felony and isn't likely to cause death or serious injury, or that it was criminally negligent.

name: No malice
plain: Something reduces the killing below murder, so malice is absent.

name: Heat of passion on adequate provocation
plain: The person's state of mind was so violent that it overcame reason: they couldn't think well enough to form a deliberate purpose or control their actions. Mere anger isn't enough. It follows adequate provocation, meaning anything that would naturally produce that passion in a person of average mind and disposition, and the act comes soon after.
note: Follows N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206.10, 206.30A and 206.40. In a murder case the State has to disprove heat of passion; if it can't, the most that remains is voluntary manslaughter.

name: Imperfect self-defense
plain: The person acted in self-defense but used more force than the law allows, or was the one who started the fight without meaning to kill when it began.
note: Follows N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206.10 (the voluntary manslaughter instruction on excessive force and the aggressor). Replaces an earlier draft wording based on honest belief, which the instruction doesn't use.

name: Unlawful act (not a felony) or criminal negligence
plain: The death came from breaking the law in a way that isn't a felony, or from criminal negligence: carelessness so serious it amounts to heedless indifference to other people's safety and rights.
note: Wording follows the 206 series (206.10, 206.30A, 206.40, 206.50), which say 'criminal negligence'; older cases may say 'culpable negligence'. The act, intentional or not, must not itself be a felony or likely to result in death or great bodily harm. An act like that done in passion or imperfect self-defense is voluntary manslaughter, never involuntary (206.10, n.21, citing State v. Ray).

name: Breaking and entering
plain: The person both breaks in and goes inside. A breaking can be physical, or by threat of force, or by a trick that gets someone to open the way in. An entry can be with any part of the body or a tool the person controls.
note: The statute says 'break and enter'. Burglary needs both. Meanings of breaking and entering follow N.C.P.I.-Crim. 214.10, nn.1-2, which are case-law definitions.

name: No consent from the owner or tenant
plain: The owner or tenant didn't agree to the person breaking in or going in.
note: Listed as its own thing the State must prove in N.C.P.I.-Crim. 214.10, 214.34 and 214.47. Missing from the first drafts.

name: Breaking or entering
plain: The person breaks in or goes in. Either one is enough. A breaking can be by threat of force or a trick, and an entry can be with any part of the body or a tool.
note: Same meanings as in N.C.P.I.-Crim. 214.10, nn.1-2.

name: A home or sleeping room
plain: Someone else's home, including other buildings used as part of it and close by (like a kitchen or smokehouse in the yard), or a room used for sleeping.
note: The statute says 'dwelling house or room used as a sleeping apartment of another'. How far 'dwelling house' reaches comes from State v. Green, cited in N.C.P.I.-Crim. 214.10, n.3.

name: A building
plain: Includes homes, empty houses, buildings under construction, buildings within the curtilage of a home (the yard area around it), and other structures designed to house or secure activities or property.

name: Intent to commit a felony or larceny inside
plain: When the person gets in, they plan to commit a serious crime (a felony) or to steal something inside.
note: The statutes say 'intent to commit any felony or larceny'. Any larceny counts by those words. N.C.P.I.-Crim. 214.10 says 'felony' and treats larceny as an example.

name: No plan to commit a felony or steal
plain: The person doesn't plan a felony or theft inside.

name: Intent to terrorize or injure an occupant
plain: The person means to terrorize (fill with terror) or injure someone inside the building.
note: 'Terrorize' is defined in N.C.P.I.-Crim. 214.47, n.2, from case law.

name: No intent to terrorize or injure
plain: The person doesn't mean to scare or hurt anyone inside.

name: Wrongful entry
plain: The person acted wrongfully, without any claim of right to be there.
note: The statute says 'wrongfully'. N.C.P.I.-Crim. 214.34 explains it as 'without any claim of right'.

name: Someone inside at the time
plain: A person is actually inside some part of the home or sleeping room while it happens.

name: Nobody inside at the time
plain: No one is actually inside the home or sleeping room while it happens.

name: Taking and carrying away another's property
plain: The person takes someone else's property and carries it away (even the slightest movement counts), without the owner's consent, knowing they aren't entitled to it and meaning to deprive the owner of it permanently. Taking it only temporarily isn't enough.
note: The pattern instructions (216.05, 216.10) list these as five separate things; they are combined here. A footnote on temporary deprivation says to compare State v. Smith.

name: A special circumstance that makes it a felony
plain: The larceny falls into one of the situations the statute makes a felony whatever the value: taken from a person; taken as part of a burglary or breaking or entering offense (including breaking out of a home, breaking into a place of worship, and burglary with explosives); the property is an explosive or incendiary device or substance; the property is a firearm; the property is a record or paper in the custody of the State Archives; or the person has at least four earlier larceny convictions.
note: G.S. 14-72(b)(1)-(6). The statute's list is complete as written here. Counting the earlier convictions has rules: the person must have had a lawyer or waived one, and several convictions in one court session or week count once unless the offenses were in different counties. Fireworks and ordinary fuels such as gasoline and natural gas don't count as explosive or incendiary substances; air rifles and air pistols don't count as firearms.

name: No special circumstance
plain: None of the felony-regardless-of-value situations applies.

name: Property worth more than $1,000
plain: The stolen property is worth more than $1,000. If the value is in doubt, the jury sets it in its verdict.

name: Property worth $1,000 or less
plain: The stolen property is worth $1,000 or less.

name: An assault on another person
plain: An intentional act that applies force, however slight, to another person's body without consent, or an intentional attempt or show of force that would make a person of reasonable firmness fear immediate bodily harm.
note: From N.C.P.I.-Crim. 120.20, which gives several definitions depending on whether there is a physical touching. Self-defense and other justifications are separate instructions (308 series) and aren't modeled.

name: Actually touching or striking the victim
plain: The person doesn't just threaten. They actually make unwanted physical contact.
note: Needed where the statute says 'assault and battery'. Wording needs review.

name: Use of a deadly weapon
plain: A weapon likely to cause death or serious bodily injury. A jury looks at what the object is, how it was used, and the size and strength of the person using it compared with the victim.
note: The statutes use the term without defining it. The definition and factors follow N.C.P.I.-Crim. 208.15.

name: No deadly weapon
plain: No deadly weapon was used.

name: Serious injury
plain: Physical injury that causes great pain and suffering.
note: Not the same as 'serious bodily injury' in G.S. 14-32.4, which the statute defines. The definition comes from cases cited in N.C.P.I.-Crim. 208.15, n.4; a judge may tell the jury that an obviously severe injury is serious.

name: No serious injury
plain: The victim wasn't seriously injured.

name: Serious bodily injury
plain: Injury that creates a substantial risk of death, causes serious permanent disfigurement or a coma, causes a permanent or long-lasting condition with extreme pain, causes permanent or long-lasting loss or impairment of the function of a body part or organ, or results in prolonged hospitalization.

name: No serious bodily injury
plain: The injury doesn't meet the statute's definition of serious bodily injury.

name: Physical injury by strangulation
plain: The assault injures the victim by strangling them: outside pressure on the neck closes blood vessels or air passages. Complete closure isn't needed, but there must be enough pressure that the victim had difficulty breathing. 'Physical injury' means hurt, damage, or loss to the body.
note: From N.C.P.I.-Crim. 208.61, nn.1 and 4. The definition of physical injury comes from an unpublished appellate decision cited there.

name: No strangulation injury
plain: The injury wasn't caused by strangulation.

name: No other law punishes it more
plain: If another law punishes the same conduct more harshly, that law applies instead.

name: The victim is an emergency worker
plain: A law enforcement officer, firefighter, emergency medical technician, or medical responder.
note: G.S. 14-32(f) names four groups and defines none of them. 'Medical responder' in particular has no definition in this section.

name: The victim is not an emergency worker
plain: The victim isn't a law enforcement officer, firefighter, EMT, or medical responder.

name: The victim is in a protected group
plain: Examples: a woman assaulted by a man at least 18, a pregnant woman, a child under 12, a government employee on duty, a school employee or volunteer on duty, a public transit operator, a company or campus police officer, or a rideshare driver working.

name: The victim is not in a protected group
plain: None of the protected categories applies.

name: Female victim, male offender at least 18
plain: A man at least 18 years old assaults a woman or girl.

name: The victim is pregnant
plain: The person assaults a pregnant woman.

name: The victim is a child under 12
plain: The person assaults a child younger than 12.

name: The victim is a government officer or employee on duty
plain: A State or local government officer or employee doing official duties.

name: The victim is a school employee or volunteer on duty
plain: An employee of a school board, charter school or registered nonpublic school; an independent contractor (or its employee) who does work schools' own employees customarily do; or an adult volunteer supervised by one of them. The assault is on them while doing their duties, or because of their duties. 'Duties' covers all activities on school property, school-authorized events (and getting students to or from them), and school transportation.
note: G.S. 14-33(c)(6). G.S. 14-33(c1) separately protects school personnel who take reasonable good-faith action to end a fight between students from civil or criminal liability.

name: The victim is a public transit operator on duty
plain: A public transit operator doing their job.

name: The victim is a company or campus police officer on duty
plain: A certified company police officer or campus police officer doing their duties.

name: The victim is a rideshare driver working
plain: A transportation network company driver providing rideshare service.

name: The victim is a sports official on duty
plain: An umpire, referee, coach or similar person who enforces the rules or supervises players at an organized athletic event (school, college, community, business, nonprofit, professional or semiprofessional), doing their duties at the event or right after it.
note: N.C.P.I.-Crim. 208.14 (2011) lists only an assault. G.S. 14-33(b)(9), read in full on 2026-10-17, says 'assault and battery', so the statute is followed here.

name: The victim is a utility or communications worker on duty
plain: A worker for a company that provides electricity, natural gas, liquid petroleum, water, wastewater, phone or internet service (an employee, an agent, or someone under contract with it), assaulted while doing their duties and while readily identifiable as a worker. Wearing a uniform, hat or outerwear with the company's logo counts, but the statute says the term 'includes' that, so it isn't the only way.
note: G.S. 14-33(b)(10), added by S.L. 2025-71, s. 1(a), for offenses committed on or after Dec 1, 2025. The statute applies to companies that are State-created or privately, municipally, county or cooperatively owned.

name: A personal relationship with the victim
plain: A relationship covered by the domestic violence law, G.S. 50B-1(b): current or former spouses; people who live or have lived together (the statute says 'of opposite sex'); parent and child (including someone acting in place of a parent) or grandparent and grandchild; people with a child in common; current or former household members; or people in a dating relationship (the statute says 'of the opposite sex'), meaning romantically involved over time and on a continuous basis. A casual acquaintance is not a dating relationship.
note: G.S. 14-33(d)(1) points to G.S. 50B-1(b). That definition was read in full on 2026-10-17 and is quoted as published. The wording about the sex of the parties is shown as the statute states it; this tool doesn't evaluate how it is applied. G.S. 50B-1 is not yet among the sections the change checker watches.

name: In the presence of a minor
plain: A minor was in a position to see or hear the assault. A minor is a person under 18 who lives with, or is under the care and supervision of, and has a personal relationship with, the person assaulted or the person who committed the assault.
note: G.S. 14-33(d)(2) and (3). N.C.P.I.-Crim. 208.72 follows the same definitions.

name: Pointing a gun or pistol at another person
plain: The person intentionally points a gun at someone. It doesn't matter whether it is loaded, or whether it is done as a joke.
note: G.S. 14-34 says only 'point any gun or pistol at any person'. The statute's text has no intent word and lists no exceptions. The plain-language wording follows N.C.P.I.-Crim. 208.85.

name: Castration, or cutting off, maiming or disfiguring the private parts
plain: Castrating another person, or cutting off, maiming or disfiguring any of their private (genital) parts.

name: Malice aforethought
plain: The act is done with malice aforethought. The statute uses the term without defining it.
note: The homicide element 'Malice' explains the term in murder cases; it may not carry over exactly to these sections. No pattern jury instruction was read for this term.

name: On purpose and unlawfully, but without malice aforethought
plain: The act is done on purpose and unlawfully, but not with malice aforethought.

name: Intent to murder, maim, disfigure, disable or render impotent
plain: The person meant to murder, maim, disfigure, disable or render the victim impotent.

name: Intent to kill, maim, disfigure, disable or render impotent
plain: The person meant to kill, maim, disfigure, disable or render the victim impotent.

name: Intent to murder, maim or disfigure
plain: The person meant to murder, maim or disfigure the victim.

name: Cutting the nose, or cutting or biting off the nose, a lip or an ear
plain: Cutting or slitting the nose, or biting or cutting off the nose, a lip or an ear.

name: Disabling a limb or member
plain: Disabling any limb or member of another person.

name: Cutting out or disabling the tongue, or putting out an eye
plain: Unlawfully cutting out or disabling another person's tongue, or putting out an eye.

name: Throwing corrosive acid or alkali on a person
plain: Knowingly and willfully throwing, or causing to be thrown, corrosive acid or alkali on another person.

name: Done maliciously
plain: The act is done maliciously. The statute doesn't define the word.
note: No pattern jury instruction was read for this term.

name: Done in a secret manner
plain: The assault is committed in a secret manner, such as by waylaying the victim. It is enough that the victim knew the attacker was nearby.

name: The victim is a child under 18
plain: The child is younger than 18.

name: Circumcising, excising or infibulating the genitals of a child
plain: Circumcising, excising or infibulating the whole or any part of the labia majora, labia minora or clitoris, knowingly and unlawfully.
note: A surgical operation is not a violation if it is necessary to the person's health and done by a licensed medical practitioner, or done on a person in labor who has just given birth for medical purposes connected with the labor or birth by a licensed practitioner, certified nurse midwife, or a person training for either (G.S. 14-28.1(e)). It is no defense that anyone believes it is required by custom or ritual, or that the person consented (G.S. 14-28.1(f)).

name: A parent, or a person who provides care to or supervises the child
plain: The person is the child's parent, or provides care to or supervises the child.

name: Consenting to or permitting the procedure
plain: Consenting to, or permitting, the unlawful circumcision, excision or infibulation of the child.

name: Removing the child from the State for the procedure
plain: Knowingly removing the child from North Carolina, or permitting the child's removal, for the purpose of having the procedure done.

name: The victim is an individual with a disability
plain: A person with a physical or mental disability (such as decreased use of arms or legs, blindness, deafness, intellectual disability or mental illness) or an infirmity, that would substantially impair the ability to defend oneself.

name: A deadly weapon, or other force likely to inflict serious injury
plain: Uses a deadly weapon or other means of force likely to inflict serious injury or serious damage to the individual with a disability.

name: Serious injury or serious damage
plain: Inflicts serious injury or serious damage to the individual with a disability.
note: The statute doesn't define 'serious injury or serious damage'.

name: The victim is a patient or resident of a care facility
plain: A patient of a health care facility (hospitals, nursing and other care facilities, psychiatric and rehabilitation facilities, home health agencies, and similar facilities) or a resident of a residential care facility (adult care homes and similar facilities), public or private.

name: Physical abuse that results in death or bodily injury
plain: Physical abuse of a patient or resident that results in death or bodily injury. 'Abuse' means the willful or culpably negligent infliction of physical injury, or the willful or culpably negligent violation of any law designed for the health or welfare of a patient or resident.

name: Intentional conduct proximately causes death
plain: Intentional conduct proximately causes the patient's or resident's death.
note: 'Proximately causes' isn't defined in the statute.

name: Culpably negligent conduct proximately causes death
plain: Culpably negligent conduct proximately causes the patient's or resident's death. 'Culpably negligent' means conduct of a willful, gross and flagrant character, showing reckless disregard of human life.

name: Willful or culpably negligent conduct
plain: The conduct is willful or culpably negligent.

name: A pattern of conduct
plain: The conduct shows a pattern of conduct.
note: The statute doesn't say how many acts make a pattern.

name: Bodily injury to the patient or resident
plain: The conduct proximately causes bodily injury to the patient or resident.

name: A caretaker of a disabled or elder adult living in a home setting
plain: The person is a caretaker, meaning they are responsible for the adult's care because of a family relationship or because they took on the care voluntarily or by contract. The adult is disabled (18 or older, or a lawfully emancipated minor, and physically or mentally incapacitated as defined in G.S. 108A-101(d)) or elderly (60 or older and unable to arrange the services needed to protect their rights and resources and maintain their well-being). The adult lives in a home setting, meaning any residence other than a health care facility or residential care facility as defined in G.S. 14-32.2.

name: Malice aforethought, knowingly and willfully
plain: The person acts with malice aforethought, knowingly and willfully.
note: The statute doesn't define malice aforethought here. No pattern jury instruction was read for this term.

name: Wantonly, recklessly, or with gross carelessness
plain: The person acts wantonly, recklessly, or with gross carelessness.
note: The statute doesn't define these terms. No pattern jury instruction was read for this term.

name: Assaults the adult
plain: The caretaker assaults the disabled or elder adult.

name: Fails to provide medical or hygienic care
plain: The caretaker fails to provide medical or hygienic care.

name: Confines or restrains in a cruel or unsafe place or condition
plain: Confines or restrains the adult in a place or under a condition that is cruel or unsafe.

name: Confines or restrains in an unsafe place or condition
plain: Confines or restrains the adult in a place or under a condition that is unsafe.

name: The adult suffers mental or physical injury
plain: As a result of the act or failure to act, the adult suffers mental or physical injury.

name: The adult suffers serious injury
plain: As a result of the act or failure to act, the adult suffers serious injury.
note: The statute doesn't define 'serious injury' here.

name: Uses or attempts physical force, or threatens use of a deadly weapon
plain: Uses or attempts to use physical force, or threatens the use of a deadly weapon, against another person.

name: A current or former spouse, parent or guardian of the victim
plain: The person is a current or former spouse, parent, or guardian of the victim.

name: Shares a child in common with the victim
plain: The person shares a child in common with the victim.

name: Lives or has lived with the victim as a spouse, parent or guardian
plain: The person is cohabitating with, or has cohabitated with, the victim as a spouse, parent, or guardian.

name: Similarly situated to a spouse, parent or guardian
plain: The person is similarly situated to a spouse, parent, or guardian of the victim.
note: The statute doesn't say what 'similarly situated' covers.

name: A current or recent former dating relationship
plain: The person has a current or recent former dating relationship with the victim. The statute says 'dating relationship' is defined in the federal law 18 U.S.C. § 921, not in G.S. 14-32.5.

name: A current offense under G.S. 14-32.5, or an assault on a related person
plain: The person commits an offense under G.S. 14-32.5, or commits an assault on someone related to them by one of the relationship descriptions in G.S. 14-32.5.

name: Two earlier qualifying convictions, the earlier within 15 years
plain: Two or more earlier convictions in one of two combinations: (1) two or more convictions under G.S. 14-32.5, or a substantially similar offense in another jurisdiction; or (2) one conviction of that kind plus at least one conviction, in North Carolina or elsewhere, for an assault on a person related to them by a G.S. 14-32.5 relationship. The earlier of the two convictions must have been no more than 15 years before the current violation.

name: A current qualifying assault offense
plain: The person violates G.S. 14-33 and causes physical injury, or violates G.S. 14-32.5 or G.S. 14-34.

name: Two earlier assault convictions, the earlier within 15 years
plain: Two or more earlier convictions for misdemeanor assault, felony assault, or a violation of G.S. 14-32.5, with the earlier of the two convictions no more than 15 years before the current violation.

name: Willfully or wantonly discharging a firearm or barreled weapon
plain: Willfully or wantonly discharging, or attempting to discharge, a firearm or barreled weapon capable of firing shot, bullets, pellets or other missiles at a muzzle velocity of at least 600 feet per second.

name: Into occupied property
plain: The discharge is into a building, structure, vehicle, aircraft, watercraft, or other conveyance, device, equipment, erection or enclosure while it is occupied.

name: Into an occupied dwelling or an occupied vehicle in operation
plain: The discharge is into an occupied dwelling, or into an occupied vehicle, aircraft, watercraft or other conveyance that is in operation.

name: At or into an unoccupied emergency vehicle
plain: The discharge is at or into an unoccupied emergency vehicle: law enforcement, fire department, ambulance, rescue squad, State or local emergency management, National Guard, U.S. Armed Forces, Department of Adult Correction, or Division of Juvenile Justice vehicles.

name: Discharging from inside an enclosure toward people outside it
plain: Willfully or wantonly discharging, or attempting to discharge, a firearm from within a building, structure, motor vehicle, or other conveyance, erection or enclosure, toward a person or persons not within it.

name: As part of criminal gang activity
plain: The discharge is part of criminal gang activity. G.S. 14-34.9 doesn't define the term itself.
note: A definition may exist elsewhere in the statutes but wasn't looked up for this record. No pattern jury instruction was read for this term.

name: Discharging a firearm inside an occupied enclosure
plain: Willfully or wantonly discharging, or attempting to discharge, a firearm within an occupied building, structure, motor vehicle, or other conveyance, erection or enclosure.

name: Intent to incite fear in another
plain: The person meant to make another person afraid.

name: The victim is a law enforcement, probation or parole officer on duty
plain: A law enforcement officer, probation officer, or parole officer who is discharging or attempting to discharge official duties.

name: The victim is a National Guard member on duty
plain: A member of the North Carolina National Guard who is discharging or attempting to discharge official duties.

name: The victim is a detention facility employee on duty
plain: A person employed at a detention facility operated under the jurisdiction of the State or a local government, who is performing their duties.

name: An assault with a firearm
plain: An assault committed with a firearm.
note: The statute doesn't define 'firearm' in this section. No pattern jury instruction was read for this term.

name: Physical injury, including cuts, scrapes and bruises
plain: Physical injury, which includes cuts, scrapes, bruises, or other physical injury that is not serious injury.

name: The victim is a health care worker, firefighter or hospital worker on duty
plain: An emergency medical technician or other emergency health care provider; a medical responder; a hospital employee, medical practice employee, licensed health care provider, or individual under contract to provide services at a hospital or medical practice; a firefighter; or hospital security personnel. They must be discharging or attempting to discharge their official duties.

name: An assault or affray causing physical injury
plain: An assault or affray that causes physical injury.
note: 'Physical injury' isn't defined in G.S. 14-34.6 itself. No pattern jury instruction was read for this term.

name: A deadly weapon other than a firearm
plain: The person uses a deadly weapon that is not a firearm.

name: Uses a firearm
plain: The person uses a firearm.

name: Intentionally pointing a laser device that is emitting a beam
plain: Intentionally pointing a laser device while it is emitting a laser beam.

name: At a law enforcement officer or other listed worker on duty
plain: At a law enforcement officer; probation or parole officer; a person whose duties include custody, transportation or management of detained or confined persons; a firefighter; an emergency medical technician or other emergency health care provider; a National Guard member; a member of the U.S. Armed Forces; or a court counselor with juvenile intake, probation, post-release supervision or court supervision duties. They must be performing their duties.

name: At the head or face of another person
plain: At the head or face of any person not covered by the list of workers.

name: At a law enforcement or search and rescue animal on duty
plain: At a law enforcement agency animal or a search and rescue animal while it is performing its duty.

name: The animal is caused 'harm'
plain: The animal is caused 'harm' as G.S. 14-163.1 defines that term.

name: Importing, making, possessing, selling or otherwise handling a teflon-coated bullet
plain: Importing, manufacturing, possessing, storing, transporting, selling, offering to sell, purchasing, offering to purchase, delivering, giving to another, or acquiring a teflon-coated bullet.
note: Exceptions in G.S. 14-34.3(b): armed forces and some officers acting in official duty; licensed importers, manufacturers and dealers who possess only to sell to authorized law enforcement; and people employed by or under contract with a manufacturer doing research on police-type body armor.

name: Adulterating or misbranding, or selling adulterated or misbranded, food, drugs or cosmetics
plain: Manufacturing, selling, delivering, offering or holding for sale an adulterated or misbranded food, drug or cosmetic, or adulterating or misbranding one, in violation of G.S. 106-122.

name: Intent to cause serious injury or death
plain: The person meant to cause serious injury or death.

name: Telling another that they have done, or will do, the adulteration
plain: Communicating to another that the person has violated, or intends to violate, G.S. 14-34.4(a).

name: Intent to wrongfully obtain something of value, or an acquittance, advantage or immunity
plain: The person meant to wrongfully obtain, directly or indirectly, anything of value or any acquittance, advantage, or immunity.
